text: Same rules as the classic house-robbing problem — you can't rob two adjacent houses — but now the houses are arranged in a circle. The first house and the last house are neighbors too. Return the most you can rob.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the only new rule versus the linear version is that house zero and house n minus one now count as adjacent, so I can't take both. Everything else is the same?
Exactly. And the array has at least one house.

Let me run through an example: two, seven, nine, three, one. The linear answer would grab houses zero, two and four, for two plus nine plus one, twelve. But on a circle, houses zero and four are neighbors, so that's illegal. Dropping one end, the best legal grab is houses zero and two, for eleven. So the answer is eleven, one less than the linear case.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. I don't want to rewrite a whole circular DP. This problem reminds me of the take-or-skip linear DP: each house is either robbed, on top of the best from two houses back, or skipped, keeping the best from one house back. The one new constraint is not both ends. That means at least one end goes unrobbed. So I can reduce the circle to two linear runs: one that excludes the last house, one that excludes the first — then take the max. Each run is just the one-D DP I already know.

Here's the plan. One: if there's only one house, return it — it has no neighbor at all. Two: run the linear DP on houses zero through n minus two, keeping the head and dropping the tail. Three: run it again on houses one through n minus one, dropping the head, and return the larger result. One thing worth flagging — two runs is enough, not three. Rob neither end is already contained in both ranges, so it's never missed. And n equals one needs a guard, or the drop-tail range becomes empty. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it — the table version and the constant-space one.

Alright, let me code this up. In the table version, rob handles the tiny cases, then returns the max of take on the drop-tail range and take on the drop-head range. Take is the linear robber on a sub-range s to e: dp of i is the best over the first i houses of that range, so the i-th house is nums of s plus i minus one. The constant-space take is the same recurrence with two rolling variables. One thing worth flagging — compute cur first, then shift, so prev one isn't clobbered before it feeds prev two. And the rolling version needs no guard for two houses: each range is a single house, and take simply returns it.

Let's dry-run on two, seven, nine, three, one, expected eleven. Run A drops the tail and scans two, seven, nine, three. The row that matters is the nine: robbing it on top of the two beats skipping it, so eleven. Run B drops the head and scans seven, nine, three, one, ending at ten. The max of eleven and ten is eleven. That matches. The circle costs exactly the one at the tail, because taking both ends, houses zero and four, is now illegal. Corner cases: one house returns itself; two houses return the larger, since they're neighbors.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — two linear passes, two n, and the constant drops. Space is linear for the table, constant for the rolling version. Oh, one more thing — the reusable idea here is isolate the seam: a circular constraint becomes a small enumeration over the seam, and each choice collapses to a linear problem I already solved. If the houses formed a tree instead, the array DP breaks, and I'd switch to a post-order tree DP that returns a rob value and a skip value per node.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reduced the circle to two linear runs and argued why two is enough — at least one end is free. You guarded n equals one so the drop-tail range isn't empty. And you gave the constant-space version plus the tree-DP follow-up. Good work.
